title: Why the Spinal Cord Does Not Regrow

scenes.visual: Title card: Why the Spinal Cord Does Not Regrow.

scenes.tts: Cut a nerve in your arm, and its axons can grow back. Injure your spinal cord, and they mostly do not. That is why a spinal cord injury usually leaves a lasting loss. Two things hold central axons back. The tissue around them blocks regrowth. And adult central neurons turn their own growth program down. In a nerve of the arm, the neuron is ready to grow, and the cells around it help.
scenes.visual: Split frame. Left, a nerve in an arm: a cut axon regrows a gold growth cone through a tube of sage Schwann cells. Right, a spinal cord: the cut axon's tip stays blunt. Two labels appear on the right: 'surroundings block' and 'growth program turned down'.

scenes.tts: How do we know both matter? In rats, a peripheral nerve graft, set as a bridge from the medulla to the spinal cord, let central axons grow about thirty millimetres, until they met central tissue again. In mice, deleting a gene called P TEN from neurons of the eye let many axons regrow through a crushed optic nerve.
scenes.visual: A rat brainstem and spinal cord joined by a graft bridge; axons grow along the bridge and stop just after re-entering central tissue. Then an eye with its optic nerve crushed; a PTEN chip is crossed out in the neuron and axons pass the crush.

scenes.tts: A cut splits each axon in two. The part joined to the cell body can grow a new tip. The part beyond the cut falls to pieces after about a day and a half, by a program of its own. In mice that lack a gene called Sarm one, cut axons stay whole for weeks.
scenes.visual: A cut axon: the part joined to the cell body sprouts a growth cone; the part beyond the cut stays whole briefly, then breaks into beads. A second row labelled Sarm1 deleted keeps its stump whole.

scenes.tts: An enzyme called N M N A T two is short-lived, and the cell body must keep sending it down the axon. A cut stops the supply. Its raw material, N M N, builds up and, in the leading model, switches Sarm one on. Sarm one cleaves N A D plus. Energy fails, calcium rises, and calpains cut the axon apart.
scenes.visual: Teal NMNAT2 packets travel down the axon and are blocked by the cut; an NMN bar rises; a clamp-shaped SARM1 opens and cuts NAD+ chips; calcium dots fill the axon; calpain chips cut the scaffold; beads.

scenes.tts: In a nerve of the arm, Schwann cells, the glia of peripheral nerve, turn into repair cells. They help clear the old myelin, call in macrophages from the blood, and line up into tubes that guide the regrowing axon back toward its target, often at around a millimetre a day.
scenes.visual: Schwann cells around the cut nerve change colour to a repair state; macrophages enter from a blood vessel and take up myelin fragments; the Schwann cells line up into a tube and a growth cone advances along it toward a muscle.

scenes.tts: In the spinal cord, debris clears slowly. Proteins in central myelin, such as Nogo, collapse growth cones, though removing them alone does little. The lesion also fills with growth-blocking molecules. Astrocytes form a border around it, but that border also limits the spread of damage. So the aim is to change the scar, not remove it.
scenes.visual: In the cord, myelin debris lingers; Nogo chips touch a growth cone and it collapses; proteoglycan dots fill the lesion; a ring of astrocytes encircles it and holds spreading damage inside the ring.

scenes.tts: So there are two problems. Blocking Sarm one can keep axons from breaking down, but a fully severed stump cannot rejoin its cell body. Function returns only if the attached part regrows and connects with the right target. In rodents, each fix helps, usually partly. None yet restores function reliably in people.
scenes.visual: Two panels. Left: a SARM1 blocker keeps a severed stump whole, but a gap to the cell body remains. Right: the attached axon regrows to a muscle and forms a contact. Below, two tags: 'rodents: partly' and 'people: not yet'.
